# Tinder Verification: Real connections with real people powered by World ID

Mark Kantor is Chief Product Officer at Tinder. At Lift Off, Tinder announced the expansion of its World ID integration to the United States, bringing proof of human to one of the world's largest dating markets. The team sat down with Mark to discuss why trust is a product-level priority for Tinder, what the pilot in Japan revealed, and what comes next.

## Why are trust and authenticity so important for Tinder at this particular moment?

Tinder only works if people feel like they’re actually connecting with a real human. That sounds obvious, but today’s world is shaped so heavily by AI. It’s created awesome opportunities but also real challenges. There’s synthetic content across the internet, there are bots, and it’s hard to know sometimes who is real and who isn’t. It’s absolutely critical to Tinder’s mission that every single user on the platform knows there’s a real person behind every profile they see.

# Tinder and Zoom offer 'proof of humanity' eye-scans to combat AI

17 April 2026

Kali Hays Technology reporter

Reuters

Tinder will let users prove they are human and not robots by bringing advanced eye-scanning technology to the app amid rising fears over AI.

Users of the dating app, as well as other major platforms such as video calling service Zoom, will be able to scan their irises to earn a "proof of humanity" badge attached to their profile or name.

Through either an online app or an orb-shaped scanning device run by the World network people can submit to a scan of their iris, the coloured portion of the eye, in order to confirm they are human.

World, formerly known as Worldcoin, is part of Tools for Humanity, a start-up co-founded and chaired by Sam Altman, who is also the head of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI.

Once a person is confirmed as human by the technology they receive a unique identification code, which is stored on their smartphone and considered their World ID.

A new World ID app, as well as the partnerships with Tinder and Zoom, were revealed during a live event in San Francisco on Friday.

It began with a video projected on several large screens in a small auditorium depicting several famous journalists, including Walter Cronkite, Dan Rather, and Larry King, as well as former US President Ronald Regan.

You match with someone on a dating app and want to know if the connection is real. You read a comment thread and suspect half the accounts are bots. These are not edge cases. They are the everyday internet, and they share a common thread: the platforms people rely on for connection, competition, and culture are constantly evolving new ways to confirm that the person on the other end is, in fact, a person.

World is bringing proof of human into the platforms where people spend their time. From dating to live events to gaming, World ID is becoming the trust layer underpinning the experiences that matter most.

# World ID Verified-Human Badge Goes Global on Tinder

 Mobile ID World Editorial Team · April 21, 2026 · 2 min read 

 

Tinder has rolled out World ID’s verified-human badge globally, extending a pilot that began in Japan to users in the United States and other markets. The global availability was announced as part of World’s Lift Off event on April 17, 2026, and gives Tinder users who have verified at a World Orb a profile badge on their mobile dating profile that signals a real, unique person is behind the account.

Verification through World ID is optional for Tinder users. Those who have completed Orb enrollment can link their World ID to their Tinder account from inside the Tinder mobile app and receive the Verified Human badge on their profile, visible to others browsing and matching. The underlying biometric data stays inside World’s attestation layer, with Tinder receiving a proof that the account is tied to a unique verified human rather than a payload of biometric or personal identifiers — a separation that matters on a consumer surface where users are cautious about handing biometric data to a dating app directly.

## The Dating Apps Trust Crisis

Romance fraud costs victims $1.3 billion annually. Catfishing and fake profiles destroy user trust. 30-50% of profiles on some platforms are suspected fakes. The consequences extend far beyond direct financial losses. Trust erosion drives away legitimate users. Regulatory scrutiny increases. Insurance premiums rise. Brand reputation suffers. And the gap between what fraudsters can do and what traditional verification can catch grows wider every month.

Consider the current threat landscape for dating apps: AI can generate convincing fake identities in seconds. Deepfake technology can impersonate anyone on a video call. Bot networks can create thousands of accounts overnight. Document forgery tools are freely available. Voice cloning requires only three seconds of audio. The tools available to attackers have outpaced the defenses available to dating apps platforms - and the asymmetry is growing.
